parole.testo: From ach + -e- + nebbisj, from Yiddish נעביש (nebish), from נעבעך (nebekh, “poor, unfortunate”), from a Slavic language. Compare English nebbish.
Borrowed from Yiddish בית (bajes, “house”), from Hebrew בית (báyit, “house”).
From an abbreviation of Yiddish בעל־מזל (bal-mazel).
Borrowed from Yiddish בענטשן (bentshn). Doublet of benedijen.
Borrowed from Yiddish בעל־הבית (balebos), from Hebrew בַּעַל הַבַּיִת (bá'al habáyit, “master of the house”).

parole.significato: a sweet, soft pastry containing cinnamon from Zeeland, originating from European Jewish cuisine
parole.testo: Generally regarded as borrowed from Yiddish [Term?], from Ladino [Term?], from Spanish bollo or bola.
Borrowed from Yiddish בחור (bokher), from Hebrew בָּחוּר (bakhúr).
From Yiddish ברכה (brokhe), from Hebrew בְּרָכָה (brakhá).
Ultimately from Yiddish בונדיזם (bundizm), probably via German.
Ultimately from Yiddish בונדיסט (bundist), probably via German. First attested in 1906.
Borrowed from Yiddish חלה (khale), from Hebrew חַלָּה (khalá).
Borrowed from Yiddish חתונה (khasene). Doublet of chatoena.
Borrowed from Yiddish חופּה (khupe), from Hebrew חופה (khupá). Doublet of choepa.
From Yiddish כריין (khreyn), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *xrěnъ (“horseradish”).
From Yiddish דאַוונען (davnen, “to pray”).

parole.significato: to remain inconspicuous, keep a low profile, to retreat
parole.testo: From Yiddish [Term?], from Portuguese deixe.
Borrowed from Yiddish דרשה (droshe), from Hebrew דְּרָשָׁה (drashá).
Borrowed from Yiddish חבֿר (khaver, “friend”), from Hebrew חָבֵר (khavér, “friend”).
Borrowed from Yiddish גײַעס (gayes), perhaps from Hebrew גיס (gayís).

From Yiddish חלש (khallish, “nauseous”), from Hebrew חַלָשׁ (chalash, “weak”). Said to be used in theatre circles originally. Probably an association with geil (“horny”) and gallig (“choleric”) has been made, whence the senses angry and hot, an instance of folk etymology.
Borrowed from Yiddish גנבֿ (ganef), from Hebrew גַּנָּב (ganáv).

parole.significato: to steal, to appropriate oneself something
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish כאַפּן (khapn, “to grab”), from Polish chapać. Attested since 1875.
Borrowed from Yiddish חן (kheyn, “grace, charm”), from Hebrew חֵן.
Borrowed from Yiddish חטאתים (khateysem), plural of חטאת (khates, “sin offering”), from Hebrew חַטָּאת (khatát, “sin offering”), from חָטָא (khatá, “to sin”).
Borrowed from Netherlandic-Yiddish pronunciation of the letter Yiddish ח (khes (neth. 'khis')), being the first letter of the Yiddish word Yiddish חכם (khokhem, “wise man, wise guy”)
From Yiddish חכמה (khokhme), from Hebrew חׇכְמָה (khokhmá, “wisdom”).

parole.significato: a goy, gentile in the Jewish sense of ethnic non-Jew
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish גוי (goy), from Hebrew גוי (“nation”).

parole.significato: goy, gentile in the Jewish sense of ethnic non-Jew
parole.testo: From Yiddish גוייִם (goyem, “gentiles”); see goj for more.

parole.significato: goy, gentile in the Jewish sense of ethnic non-Jew
parole.testo: From goj (“goy”), from Yiddish גוי (goy).
Borrowed from Yiddish [Term?].
Borrowed from Yiddish חכם (khokhem), from Hebrew חָכָם (khakhám). First attested in the year 1800.
From the Bargoens register, borrowed from Yiddish חוצפה (chotspe), from Hebrew חֻצְפָּה (ḥuṣpā), from Aramaic חוצפא. Cognate with English chutzpah and German Chuzpe.
Borrowed from Yiddish חתן (khosen), from Hebrew חָתָן (khatán, “bridegroom”).

parole.significato: trifle (something of very small importance or very low price)
parole.testo: Said to derive from Yiddish.
Via Yiddish [Term?] from Hebrew אָכַל (akhál, “to eat”).

parole.significato: a coin with the denomination of 25 guilder cents
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish ה (hey) + -tje, from Hebrew ה, the fifth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The kwartje had a value of five stuivers (each stuiver being worth 5 cents, for a total of 25 cents per kwartje). Compare the obsolete vijfje for the same coin.
Derived from Yiddish [script needed] (hourek) via Bargoens, from Hebrew חוֹרֵג (hureg, “criminal, step-”).
From Yiddish עבר ובטל (over u-batl).
Borrowed from Yiddish יין (yayin, “wine”), from Hebrew יַיִן (yáyin, “wine”).
Borrowed from Yiddish יד (yad, “hand”) from Hebrew יָד (yāḏ, “hand”).

parole.significato: the first cash a merchant receives on a day
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish יד מעות (yad mo('e)s). The sense “thief” is a much later development from jatmozen (“to engage in petty theft”).
From Yiddish יד (yad, “hand”), ידיים (yadáyim, “two hands”).
Borrowed from Yiddish ייִדיש (yidish, “Jewish, Yiddish”).

parole.significato: tenner, banknote of ten monetary units (usually guilders or euros)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish י (yud, “yod (tenth letter of the alphabet)”), from Hebrew י.
Borrowed from Yiddish יפה (yofe), from Hebrew יָפֶה (yāfé).

parole.significato: an inmate of a Nazi concentration camp
parole.testo: From Yiddish, (KZ-nik, Kazetnik, Katsetnik, ק. צטניק (k. tstnik)) (Yiddish for inmate of a Nazi concentration camp); derived from the abbreviation KZ (pronounced as Kah-Tzet) for the German word Konzentrationslager by the addition of the suffix -nik of Slavic origin, which approximately corresponds
Borrowed from Yiddish [Term?].

From Yiddish כּלה (kale, “bride”), from Hebrew כַּלָּה (kalá, “bride”). A relation with the verb kallen (“to chatter”, compare etymology 2 hereunder), claimed in some popular-scientific resources, exists at most through secondary association. Compare German Kalle.
From Yiddish [Term?], from Hebrew כַּפֹּרֶת.

parole.significato: pretensions, a high opinion of oneself
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish גאַותנות (gavsones, “arrogance”), from Hebrew גאוותנות / גַּאַוְתָנוּת (ga'av'tanút, “arrogance”). Originally used by Jews from Amsterdam.
Borrowed from Yiddish קעפּל (kepl), from Middle High German keppel.
Borrowed from Yiddish קהילה (kehile, “(Jewish) community”), from Hebrew קְהִלָּה (k'hillá, “congregation”). Doublet of kehilla.
Borrowed from Yiddish קנאה ושׂנאה (kine vesine) or קנאה־שׂנאה (kine-sine), from Hebrew קִנְאָה וְשִׂנְאָה (kin'á v'sin'á).

parole.significato: cop, pig: synonym of politieagent (“police officer”)
parole.testo: Likely from Yiddish כּלבֿ (kelev, “damn dog, son of a bitch”); Yiddish ־אַק (-ak). First attested with its current meaning in 1884.

From Yiddish [Term?], from the Hebrew letters קוּ״ף (kuf) and נוּ״ן (nun) representing the phrase kost niets (“costs nothing”) (or its Yiddish equivalent). By surface analysis, koef (“qoph”) + noen (“nun”).
Borrowed from Yiddish כּשר (kosher), from Hebrew כָּשֵׁר (kashér).
From Yiddish קטן (koten, “small child”), from Hebrew קָטָן (qāṭān, “young, little”).

parole.significato: to leyn, that is, to read from a Torah scroll
parole.testo: From Yiddish לייענען (leyenen, “to read”).
Borrowed from Yiddish [Term?].
Probably from Yiddish לוויה (levaje, “funeral”), as Jewish funerals were often accompanied by a lot of wailing and clamour.
Borrowed from Yiddish לבֿ (leyv, “courage”), which is borrowed from Hebrew לב (lev, “heart”).

parole.significato: to study the Torah, Talmud or other Jewish religious writings
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish לערנען (lernen).
Possibly from the Yiddish surnames לייפּ (leyp), לייב (leyb), if originally used as a slur against Jews. Related to the surnames Leib, Leip, and Löwe, all with the meaning "lion".

parole.significato: Indicates that something is useless, unavailable or unlikely to happen.
parole.testo: From a Yiddish version of Hebrew לֹא לָנוּ (lo lánu, literally “not to/for us”).
Borrowed from Yiddish מים (mayem, “water”), from Hebrew מַיִם (máyim, “water”), from Proto-Semitic *may-, from Proto-Afroasiatic *maʔ- (“water”). Doublet of mu and mem.
From Yiddish מכה (make, “illness”), from Hebrew מַכָּה (maká, “attack”).

parole.significato: mamzer, bastard (child born from a disallowed relationship)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish ממזר (mamzer), from Hebrew מַמְזֵר (mamzér).
Borrowed from Yiddish מצה (matse), from Hebrew מַצָּה (matsá).
Borrowed from Yiddish מזל (mazl, “luck”).

parole.significato: Jewish communities in the Netherlands outside Amsterdam; the provinces, hinterland
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish מדינה (medine, “country”), from Hebrew מְדִינָה (m'diná).

parole.significato: honderdje, a 100 guilder or 100 euro banknote.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish מאה (méye), from Hebrew מֵאָה (me'á, “hundred”).
Borrowed from Yiddish משוגע (meshuge, “crazy”), derived from Hebrew מְשֻׁגָּע (meshugá, “crazy”).
From Yiddish משוגענער (meshugener).
From Yiddish מיאוס (mies).
Borrowed from Yiddish מנין (minyen), from Hebrew מִנְיָן (minyán). Doublet of minjan.
Borrowed from Yiddish משפּחה (mishpokhe), from Biblical Hebrew מִשְׁפָּחָה (mishpakhá).
Borrowed from Yiddish נאָך דער אשמדאי (nokh der ashmodey), with a shifted r due to re-analysis.
From Yiddish נעבעך (nebekh, “poor, unfortunate”), from Czech nebohý (“poor, pitied”). Compare English nebbish.
Borrowed from Yiddish נשמה (neshome, “soul”), from Hebrew נְשָׁמָה (n'shamá).

parole.significato: A broad term referring to something evil, shameful, unfortunate, ill-fated or even cursed.
parole.testo: From Yiddish [Term?], from Hebrew ניחוש (nikhúsh, “divination, conjecture”). A superstitious term that entered Dutch from Yiddish, possibly via Bargoens.

parole.significato: someone who belonged to a 1950s Dutch youth culture revolving around (light) motorcycles, similar to a greaser, raggare…
parole.testo: About 1920, from the Bargoens cant, probably from Dutch penoze. In turn again from borrowed from Yiddish פּרנסה (parnose, “life, livelihood”).

parole.significato: synonym of parasja (“parashah, weekly Torah portion”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּרשה (parshe), from Hebrew פָּרָשָׁה (parashá).
Probably from peigeren, from Yiddish פּגרן (peygern), from Yiddish פּגר (peyger, “carcass, cadaver”), from Hebrew פֶּגֶר (péger, “corpse, carcass”).
Borrowed from Yiddish פּגרן (peygern), from Yiddish פּגר (peyger, “carcass, cadaver”), from Hebrew פֶּגֶר (péger, “corpse, carcass”).
From Yiddish פּרנסה (parnose, “life, livelihood”), from Hebrew פַּרְנָסָה (parnasá).
Borrowed from Yiddish פּליטה (pleyte, “escape, getaway”). Compare German pleite.
Borrowing from Yiddish פּנים (ponem, “face”) from Hebrew פָּנִים (paním, “face”).
Borrowed from Yiddish פּנים (ponem, “face”) from Hebrew פָּנִים (pāním, “face”). First attested in Bargoens in 1875. See also ponem.
From Yiddish ראַמש (ramsh). Attested since 1918.

parole.significato: an Ashkenazi rabbi, in particular a Chasidic one; rebbe
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish רבי (rebe).
Borrowed from Yiddish שלימיל (shlimil).
Borrowed from Yiddish שקרים (shekorem), from Hebrew שְׁקָרִים, plural of שֶׁקֶר (“lie”).

Related to Low German schurrmurr (“chaos, disorder”). Possibly from Yiddish שורים (shorim, “Oxen”) and Yiddish חמורים (khamoyrim, “Donkeys”). Unclear relationship with Turkish şur mur (“confusion”), Albanian shiri-miri/ciri-miri (“confusion”), Romani ciri-miri (“confusion”).
Borrowed from Yiddish סדר (seyder), from Hebrew סֵדֶר.
Borrowed from Yiddish שבת (shabes, “Sabbath”), from Biblical Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát, “Sabbath”).
From Yiddish שבת גוי (shabes goy). By surface analysis, sjabbes + goj.

parole.significato: shamash or gabbai, a sexton in a synagogue
parole.testo: From Yiddish שמשׂ (shames), from Hebrew שַׁמָּשׁ (shamásh).
Borrowed from Yiddish שיכּור (shiker), from Hebrew שִׁיכֹּור (šikkōr). Attested since 1914.
Borrowed from Yiddish שיקסע (shikse).

parole.significato: a schnorrer; a beggar or sponger
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שנאָרער (shnorer).
Borrowed from Yiddish שול (shul, “synagogue, school”), from Old High German scuola, which was borrowed in turn from Latin schola. Doublet of school and skorro.
Borrowed from Yiddish שוחט (shoykhet), from Hebrew שׁוֹחֵט (shokhét).
From the pseudonym Sjloume Duikelaar. The first part is Yiddish שלמה (shloyme), adapted to the Dutch word sloom (“slow, sluggish”). The second part is formed from duikelen + -aar.
Derived from a 19th century cant (Bargoens) word smeer, borrowed from Yiddish שמירה (shmire, “guard”), from Hebrew שמירה (šəmirā, “guard”).
Borrowed from Yiddish שמועס (shmues, “talk, schmooze”). Attested since 1901.

parole.significato: to schmooze, talk softly, murmur, whisper
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שמועס (shmues, “talk, schmooze”).
From Yiddish משה (moyshe, “Moses”), pronounced moushe in Western Yiddish, from Hebrew מֹשֶׁה (moshé, “Moses”).
Borrowed from Yiddish סוף (sof, “end”), from Hebrew סוֹף (sof).
Borrowed from Yiddish צרות (tsores), plural of צרה (tsore, “trouble, problem”), from Hebrew צָרָה (tsará, “trouble, tragedy, calamity”).
Borrowed from Yiddish [script needed] (shtannes, “distrust”), from Biblical Hebrew עֶשְׁתֹּנֹת (eshtonot, “thoughts”). Attested since 1937.
Borrowed from Yiddish שתיקה (shtike), from Hebrew שתיקה (shtika, “silence”), see שָׁתַק (“to be silent”). Compare regional German stiekum.
Borrowed from Yiddish טלית (tales), from Hebrew טַלִּית (tallít).
Borrowed from Yiddish טמאה (temeye, “whore; unclean”), from Hebrew טְמֵאָה (t'me'á, “unclean, impure”), feminine of טָמֵא (tamé, “unclean, impure”).
Borrowed from Yiddish טנוף (tinef), from Hebrew טִנּוּף (tinnúf, “trash”).
From Yiddish תּיפֿלה (tifle) + אמונה (emune).
Borrowed from Yiddish תּחת (tokhes, “butt”), ultimately from Hebrew תַּחַת.
Borrowed from Yiddish טרייף (treyf), from Hebrew טְרֵפָה.

parole.significato: to con, to scam, to deceive
parole.testo: Possibly from nagel (“nail”); compare (Rotwelsch) German nageln (“to fuck”). With the prefix ver-, the semantics of this word would then be comparable to verneuken (“to fuck up”). A Yiddish origin has also been supposed.

parole.significato: to mess up, screw up (intentionally disrupt)
parole.testo: From Yiddish פֿערשטערען (fershteren, “to spoil someone's fun”), from German verstören (“to disrupt”). Doublet of verstoren.
From wieberig (“zich ~ maken / ~ gaan: (Bargoens) to scarper”) + -en < Yiddish ועייִבערעח (veyiverekh) < Hebrew וַיִּבְרַח (vayivrách, “(he) fled”).
Borrowed from Yiddish זהובֿ (zoev), from Hebrew זָהוּב (zahúv, “gold coin”), related to Hebrew זָהָב (zaháv, “gold”).

From Yiddish תּשובֿה (tshuve, “answer”), from Hebrew תְּשׁוּבָה (t'shuvá, “answer”). The shift from -v- to -g- is possibly due to association with mesjogge. If so, a doublet of tesjoeva. Alternatively, via Yiddish from a Hebrew noun of the root שׁ־ג־ח (forming words relating to supervision; e.g. the
Either borrowed from German schofel from Yiddish or a direct borrowing from Yiddish שפֿל (shofl, “shabby”), from Hebrew שָׁפָל (šāfāl, “low, humble”).
